learn.mcr.eligibility.step04.text.value: Now the fan minimum, with a hand you can count. A hand whose patterns reach at least eight fan is eligible — allowed to be declared a win. Read this pictured hand: the sequences 1-2-3 and 4-5-6 of characters, 7-8-9 of circles and 2-3-4 of bamboo, with a pair of 5s of circles. The next step counts its patterns one at a time.

learn.mcr.eligibility.step05.text.value: Count the pictured hand. Every set is a sequence and the pair is a suited tile — suited means from one of the three suits: characters, circles or bamboo — which is the pattern All Chows, worth 2 fan. The hand was kept hidden and won on a thrown tile, worth 2 more fan. Its two character sequences, 1-2-3 and 4-5-6, together cover six numbers in a row, worth 1 fan. The winning tile completed the pair and was the only wait the hand had, worth 1 fan. The patterns add to 2 + 2 + 1 + 1 = 6 fan.

learn.mcr.eligibility.step06.text.value: Six fan is below the minimum of eight, so this hand cannot be declared a win yet — even if the player has also shown three flowers. The flowers would add three points, making nine points on paper, but flower points are only added after a hand is eligible, and six fan never becomes eligible. The player must keep playing and improve the hand's patterns.

learn.mcr.eligibility.step07.text.value: One special pattern covers the opposite case. If a finished hand contains no pattern at all — no sequence or triplet pattern, no concealment or wait pattern, nothing — it is awarded the pattern Chicken Hand, worth exactly 8 fan, so it can win after all. Chicken Hand never tops a hand up: a hand with patterns worth six fan, like the one you just counted, stays at six.

learn.mcr.exclusions.q-competing-arrange.value: Add the best patterns from both groupings together
Count it once, in the single legal arrangement with the higher total
Count it in whichever arrangement was declared first
Count only the sequence grouping, because sequences are checked first
One score comes from one arrangement of the tiles. When both arrangements are legal, the higher legal total is the hand's score, and no pattern from the other arrangement is added.
The rule is about wholeness: a score must come from one grouping of the tiles, never a mixture of two.
A hand's tiles can be grouped as triplets or as repeated sequences, and the two groupings earn different patterns. How is the hand counted?

learn.mcr.exclusions.q-flush-exclusion.c.value: The pattern for using no honors
The pattern for having a voided suit
Neither — Full Flush already covers both facts

learn.mcr.exclusions.q-flush-exclusion.e.value: Full Flush already includes using one suit and no honors, so the two smaller patterns that pay for those same facts are excluded. The total stays at 45 fan.

learn.mcr.exclusions.q-flush-exclusion.h.value: Ask whether the smaller patterns describe anything that the bigger pattern has not already paid for.

learn.mcr.exclusions.q-flush-exclusion.p.value: For the one-suit hand counted in this lesson, which of these is added to its 45 fan?

learn.mcr.exclusions.step01.text.value: An exclusion is a rule that a bigger pattern replaces a smaller pattern it already includes, so the smaller one is not added as well. This pictured hand shows why exclusions exist. Read it: the sequences 1-2-3, 4-5-6 and 7-8-9 of characters, a triplet of 1s of characters, and a pair of 9s of characters. Every tile is a character. The next step counts it.

learn.mcr.exclusions.step02.text.value: Count the pictured hand. Using one suit and no honors is the pattern Full Flush, worth 24 fan. Its three sequences in a row are worth 16 fan. It was kept hidden and won on a thrown tile, worth 2 fan. It uses all four copies of the 1 of characters without declaring a quad, worth 2 fan. Its triplet of 1s is a triplet of terminals, worth 1 fan. The patterns add to 24 + 16 + 2 + 2 + 1 = 45 fan.

learn.mcr.exclusions.step03.text.value: Now the exclusion. This hand uses no honors, which by itself is the pattern No Honors, worth 1 fan, and it is missing two suits, which by itself is a pattern worth 1 fan. Neither is added: Full Flush already says, in one pattern, that the hand uses exactly one suit and no honors, so paying for those same facts again would count them twice. The total stays at the 45 fan you counted.

learn.mcr.exclusions.step04.text.value: A related rule is that one hand is counted in one arrangement. The tiles in a hand can sometimes be grouped in two different ways, and the two groupings would earn different patterns. You may not take some patterns from one grouping and some from the other — the hand is counted once, in a single arrangement, and when two arrangements are both legal the one with the higher total is used.

learn.mcr.exclusions.step05.text.value: Read this pictured hand two ways. Its character tiles — three 1s, three 2s and three 3s — can be grouped as three triplets, or as the sequence 1-2-3 three times over. With the sequence 4-5-6 of circles and the pair of 7s of bamboo, both groupings complete the hand. Counted as triplets, the hand is worth 45 fan: its three triplets step up in number in one suit for 24 fan, three concealed triplets add 16, and winning while hidden on a thrown tile, its triplet of 1s, having no honors at all, and having only one tile it could finish on add the rest. The sequence grouping is worth less, so the triplet grouping is the one that counts — all 45 fan of it, and nothing from the other grouping.

learn.mcr.exclusions.title.value: Exclusions and counting each pattern once

learn.mcr.families.q-family-fixed-set.ch.value: Yes — whenever the hand is counted again
Yes — but only if the set is a sequence
Yes — but only before the next tile is thrown

learn.mcr.families.q-family-fixed-set.ex.value: A melded set is fixed for the rest of the hand. Only tiles still concealed in the hand can be arranged in different ways when the hand is counted.

learn.mcr.families.q-family-fixed-set.hi.value: Recall the rule from the claims lesson about melded sets: once a set is shown on the table, its tiles are locked into that set.

learn.mcr.families.q-family-fixed-set.pr.value: A set has been melded and shown on the table. Can its tiles later be taken apart and rearranged to make a different pattern?

learn.mcr.families.q-family-value.choice.value: Yes — patterns in the sequences family are worth double
Yes — patterns in the honors family lose one fan
Yes — but only for patterns worth more than eight fan

learn.mcr.families.q-family-value.explan.value: Families only organise the 81 patterns for learning. A pattern's fan comes from the pattern list itself and never changes with its family.

learn.mcr.families.q-family-value.hint.value: Ask what a family is for: it groups patterns by the feature they look at. Grouping is not a scoring rule.

learn.mcr.families.q-family-value.prompt.value: Does putting a pattern into a family change how many fan that pattern is worth?

learn.mcr.families.step01.text.value: The 1 and the 9 of each suit have a name: they are terminals, the numbers at the two ends of a suit. The six tiles shown here are all the terminal kinds — the 1 and 9 of characters, circles and bamboo. Several patterns are about terminals, so the word is worth having before the families.

learn.mcr.families.step02.text.value: The numbers from 2 to 8 in a suit are called simples — every suited number that is not a terminal. This row shows all the simples of circles, from the 2 to the 8. Honors are neither terminals nor simples: they are not numbered at all.

learn.mcr.families.step03.text.value: A hand that uses only two of the three suits is missing a suit, and the missing suit is called the voided suit. Read this pictured hand: characters and circles appear, with a pair of white dragons — bamboo appears nowhere, so bamboo is this hand's voided suit. Patterns about which suits and kinds a hand uses form one of the families below.

learn.mcr.families.step04.text.value: There are 81 patterns in total, and nobody learns them as one long list. They are grouped here into families — groups of patterns that look at the same kind of feature. The families are: honors; triplets and quads; sequences; tile composition, which covers suits, terminals, simples and voided suits; special structures, which change the shape of the whole hand; concealment and winning, which cover how the hand was kept and won; and small combinations, the one- and two-fan patterns that reward pairs of sets.

learn.mcr.families.step05.text.value: A family is only a way of grouping — the skill is recognising patterns inside a real hand. Read the pictured hand again: 1-2-3 of characters, 4-5-6 of circles, 7-8-9 of bamboo, three red dragons, and a pair of white dragons. Its three sequences use the number groups 1-2-3, 4-5-6 and 7-8-9 spread across three suits — a pattern from the sequences family. Its triplet of red dragons belongs to the honors family. Two families in one hand is normal.

learn.mcr.families.step06.text.value: Read this pictured hand: the sequences 1-2-3, 4-5-6 and 7-8-9 all in characters, three red dragons, and a pair of 5s of characters. Because every suited tile is a character and honors are also present, it has a pattern from the tile-composition family. Its three character sequences in a row are a pattern from the sequences family, and its dragon triplet is from the honors family — three families in one hand.

learn.mcr.families.step07.text.value: Read this pictured hand: triplets of the 3 of characters, the 5 of circles, the 7 of bamboo and the 9 of circles, with a pair of North winds. Every set is a triplet, so this hand's patterns come from the triplets and quads family. The next lessons take the families one at a time and count real hands from each.

learn.mcr.families.step08.text.value: After this lesson you can open the full reference of all 81 patterns and search it by name. Each entry gives the pattern's fan, its family, how to recognise it, and which smaller patterns it replaces. Some names in the reference use older words for the sets: in those names, a chow is a sequence, a pung is a triplet, and a kong is a quad. The names are labels — the fan and the recognition rules are what count.

learn.mcr.families.title.value: Pattern families and the pattern reference

learn.mcr.foundation.q-char-four-drill.e.value: The small number at the top of the face is 4, so this is the 4 of characters.

learn.mcr.foundation.q-char-four-drill.h.value: Read the small number at the top of the face, not the large character below it.

learn.mcr.foundation.q-char-four-drill.p.value: What number is the pictured characters tile?

learn.mcr.foundation.q-char-seven-drill..value: The small number at the top of the face is 7, so this is the 7 of characters.
For this suit, the number to read is the small one printed at the top of the face, not the large character below it.
What number is the pictured characters tile?

learn.mcr.foundation.q-honor-pick.explan.value: East and the red dragon are honors. The other three tiles belong to the characters, circles and bamboo suits.

learn.mcr.foundation.q-honor-pick.hint.value: Honors are the winds and the dragons — the tiles with no suit and no number from 1 to 9.

learn.mcr.foundation.q-honor-pick.prompt.value: Tap every honor tile in this row.

learn.mcr.foundation.q-pattern-definitio.value: A named feature of a finished hand that the scoring list recognises
Any three tiles that share a suit
The order in which the four players take their turns
A tile that another player has thrown away

learn.mcr.foundation.q-wind-east-drill.e.value: This face is the East wind, the first of the four winds in the order they were shown.

learn.mcr.foundation.q-wind-east-drill.h.value: The winds were shown in one fixed order of four. This face is the first one in that order.

learn.mcr.foundation.q-wind-east-drill.p.value: Which wind is the pictured tile?

learn.mcr.foundation.q-wind-west-drill.e.value: This face is the West wind, the third of the four winds in the order they were shown.

learn.mcr.foundation.step01.text.value: This course teaches MCR — Mahjong Competition Rules — a game of mahjong for four players, played with tiles. Start with the characters suit, shown here from 1 to 9. Each tile in this suit carries a small number at the top and a larger character below it; the number at the top is the one to read. The 5 of characters is the fifth tile in this row.

learn.mcr.foundation.step02.text.value: The second suit is circles. A circles tile is read by counting its spots: one spot is the 1, four spots are the 4, and so on up to 9. The tiles in this row run from the 1 of circles on the left to the 9 of circles on the right.

learn.mcr.foundation.step03.text.value: The third suit is bamboo. A bamboo tile is read by counting its green sticks. The one exception is the 1 of bamboo, which is drawn as a bird instead of a single stick. This row runs from the bird, the 1 of bamboo, to the 9 of bamboo.

learn.mcr.foundation.step04.text.value: Tiles with no suit and no number from 1 to 9 are honors. The first four tiles in this row are the winds, in order: East, South, West and North. The last three are the dragons: the white dragon is a plain framed face, the green dragon carries a green character, and the red dragon carries a red character. An honor can never be part of a numbered run, because it has no number.

learn.mcr.foundation.step05.text.value: There are also eight special tiles: four flowers and four seasons, each different. When you draw a flower or a season, you show it beside your tiles and immediately draw a replacement, so it never takes a place among the tiles you are building with. Each one you show adds one point — one unit of score — to a winning hand later, but only to a hand that was already good enough to win without it.

learn.mcr.foundation.step06.text.value: Tiles are joined into sets. A set is a small group of tiles that belongs together. The first kind of set is a sequence: three tiles of the same suit whose numbers count up in a row, such as the 3, 4 and 5 of circles shown here. A sequence can never mix suits, and honors can never be in one.

learn.mcr.foundation.step07.text.value: The second kind of set is a triplet: three copies of the same tile, such as the three 8s of bamboo shown here. There are four copies of every ordinary tile in the whole set of tiles, so a triplet leaves one more copy somewhere — in another player's tiles, face-up on the table, or still to be drawn.

learn.mcr.foundation.step08.text.value: A finished hand also needs a pair: two copies of the same tile, such as the two white dragons shown here. A pair is not a set — it is the one group of two that completes the shape of a winning hand.

learn.mcr.foundation.step09.text.value: Four copies of the same tile can be declared together as one set called a quad, such as the four 9s of circles shown here. A quad is still only one set, so when you declare one you draw a replacement tile to make up for the extra tile it uses.

learn.mcr.foundation.step10.text.value: Your hand is the tiles you hold. A normal winning hand has fourteen tiles: four sets and one pair. Read this pictured hand aloud: the sequences 1-2-3 of characters, 4-5-6 of circles and 7-8-9 of bamboo, then three red dragons, then a pair of white dragons. That is four sets and a pair, so the shape is complete. This same hand returns later in the course, where you will count what it is worth.

learn.mcr.foundation.step11.text.value: A pattern is a named feature of a finished hand that the scoring list recognises. Look at the pictured hand again: its three red dragons form a triplet, and a triplet of dragons is one pattern. The three sequences use the number groups 1-2-3, 4-5-6 and 7-8-9 in three different suits, which is another pattern. One finished hand usually contains several patterns at once.

learn.mcr.foundation.step12.text.value: Fan are the points that patterns are worth. Every pattern in the scoring list is worth a set number of fan, and the value of a finished hand starts by adding up the fan of all the patterns it contains. Fan are simply added together — a pattern worth eight and a pattern worth two give ten fan together.

learn.mcr.foundation.step13.text.value: A finished hand can only be declared a win if its patterns add up to at least eight fan. That minimum is checked using pattern fan alone: the points for flowers and seasons you have shown are added afterwards, and they never help a hand reach the eight fan it needs first.

learn.mcr.foundation.step16.text.value: Now read single faces on their own, with no row order to help. This characters tile stands alone: read the small number at the top of its face.

learn.mcr.foundation.step17.text.value: One more single characters face, in no particular order.

learn.mcr.foundation.step18.text.value: The winds are read by their faces too. The four winds were shown in one fixed order — East, South, West, North — and each face is different. This face stands alone.

learn.mcr.guide.a-different-legal-comple.value: A different legal completion elsewhere in the hand disqualifies the unique wait. Only one wait-type point is used.

learn.mcr.guide.a-higher-pattern-that-ne.value: A higher pattern that necessarily requires all triplets replaces this award where specified.

learn.mcr.guide.a-sequence-qualifies-onl.value: A sequence qualifies only as 123 or 789. All Terminals, All Honors and All Terminals and Honors replace it.

learn.mcr.guide.a-thrown-tile-completing.value: A thrown tile completing a triplet makes that triplet melded for this count. Excludes the all-triplets pattern and Concealed Hand.
A thrown tile completing one of these triplets makes that triplet melded for this count. Excludes the two-concealed-triplets pattern.

learn.mcr.guide.a-triplet-completed-by-a.value: A triplet completed by a thrown tile counts as melded for this count. The three- and four-concealed-triplets patterns replace it.

learn.mcr.guide.all-three-suits-must-be-.value: All three suits must be different. These sets are considered together under the non-repeat rules.

learn.mcr.guide.an-honor-pair-disqualifi.value: An honor pair disqualifies this pattern. Excludes No Honors.

learn.mcr.guide.can-combine-with-seat-wi.value: Can combine with Seat Wind for the same set when both winds are the same. Do not add a terminal/honor-triplet point for that same award.

learn.mcr.guide.claim-all-four-sets-from.value: Claim all four sets from other players' thrown tiles and win on a thrown tile that completes the pair.

learn.mcr.guide.collect-every-terminal-a.value: Collect every terminal and honor kind, then duplicate one of those thirteen kinds.

learn.mcr.guide.complete-four-triplets-o.value: Complete four triplets or quads without taking their completing tile from another player.

learn.mcr.guide.count-different-four-cop.value: Count different four-copy kinds separately, except when a higher pattern explicitly includes those copies.

learn.mcr.guide.declare-a-melded-quad-by.value: Declare a melded quad by claiming a thrown tile or adding a fourth tile to a melded triplet.

learn.mcr.guide.declare-four-identical-c.value: Declare four identical concealed tiles as a quad and take a replacement.

learn.mcr.guide.declare-four-quads-and-c.value: Declare four quads and complete the pair.

learn.mcr.guide.declare-three-quads-conc.value: Declare three quads, concealed or melded.

learn.mcr.guide.do-not-reinterpret-the-s.value: Do not reinterpret the same tiles as a triple sequence in the same scoring arrangement.

learn.mcr.guide.do-not-reuse-the-same-re.value: Do not reuse the same required combination as another instance of this pattern.

learn.mcr.guide.dragons-seat-winds-and-r.value: Dragons, seat winds and round winds use their own awards. Higher wind or terminal/honor patterns may exclude this point.

learn.mcr.guide.draw-the-last-tile-of-th.value: Draw the last tile of the wall yourself and win on it.

learn.mcr.guide.each-different-dragon-ma.value: Each different dragon may qualify until a larger dragon combination replaces the individual awards.

learn.mcr.guide.every-number-is-1-2-3-or.value: Every number is 1, 2, 3 or 4 and no honors appear.

learn.mcr.guide.every-number-is-4-5-or-6.value: Every number is 4, 5 or 6 and no honor is present.

learn.mcr.guide.every-number-is-6-7-8-or.value: Every number is 6, 7, 8 or 9 and no honors appear.

learn.mcr.guide.every-number-is-7-8-or-9.value: Every number is 7, 8 or 9 and no honor is present.

learn.mcr.guide.excludes-upper-four-and-.value: Excludes Upper Four and No Honors.

learn.mcr.guide.include-characters-circl.value: Include characters, circles, bamboo, at least one wind and at least one dragon.

learn.mcr.guide.keep-the-hand-concealed-.value: Keep the hand concealed and win by self-draw; concealed quads are permitted.

learn.mcr.guide.make-seven-pairs-of-cons.value: Make seven pairs of consecutive numbers within one suit.

learn.mcr.guide.make-seven-pairs-with-no.value: Make seven pairs with no declared sets. Four identical tiles may supply two pairs in MCR.

learn.mcr.guide.no-repeated-kind-and-no-.value: No repeated kind and no declared set. Excludes Lesser Honors and Knitted Tiles, All Types and Concealed Hand.

learn.mcr.guide.replaces-little-three-dr.value: Replaces Little Three Dragons, the two-dragon-triplets pattern and the individual dragon triplet awards.

learn.mcr.guide.replaces-seven-pairs-ful.value: Replaces Seven Pairs, Full Flush, Concealed Hand, Single Wait, No Honors and One Voided Suit.

learn.mcr.guide.replaces-the-smaller-thr.value: Replaces the smaller three-quad combinations it is made from; concealment may contribute where the rules permit.

learn.mcr.guide.requires-the-concealed-n.value: Requires the concealed nine-way base before winning; replaces Full Flush, Concealed Hand and the implied terminal-triplet award.

learn.mcr.guide.special-honor-and-knitte.value: Special honor-and-knitted hands and Thirteen Orphans already imply these categories and exclude this award.

learn.mcr.guide.the-allowed-kinds-refer-.value: The allowed kinds refer to the conventional tile faces. Excludes One Voided Suit.

learn.mcr.guide.the-entire-hand-contains.value: The entire hand contains only numbered suits.

learn.mcr.guide.the-four-sets-are-all-tr.value: The four sets are all triplets or quads, with one pair.

learn.mcr.guide.the-nine-knitted-tiles-a.value: The nine knitted tiles are a special body, not three ordinary sequences. At most one ordinary set may be declared.

learn.mcr.guide.the-same-required-sequen.value: The same required sequences cannot be split into other repeated combination awards.

learn.mcr.guide.the-three-required-seque.value: The three required sequences do not also earn Short Straight or Two Terminal Chows.

learn.mcr.guide.use-123-456-and-789-sequ.value: Use 123, 456 and 789 sequences in one suit.

learn.mcr.guide.use-four-identical-seque.value: Use four identical sequences in the same suit.

learn.mcr.guide.use-one-numbered-suit-to.value: Use one numbered suit together with honors.

learn.mcr.guide.use-the-seat-at-decision.value: Use the seat at decision time. It can combine with Prevalent Wind when both are the same wind.

learn.mcr.guide.use-three-identical-sequ.value: Use three identical sequences in the same suit.

learn.mcr.guide.use-three-sequences-in-d.value: Use three sequences in different suits whose starting numbers advance by one.

learn.mcr.guide.use-three-sequences-in-o.value: Use three sequences in one suit whose starts advance consistently by one or two.

learn.mcr.guide.use-three-triplets-in-on.value: Use three triplets in one suit with consecutive numbers.

learn.mcr.match.q-dealer-advances.explan.value: The deal moves to the next player after every hand in this game, whoever won it — there are no repeat deals.

learn.mcr.match.q-dealer-advances.hint.value: Recall the rule that keeps every round to exactly four hands: it is about how the deal moves, win, loss or drawn hand alike.

learn.mcr.match.q-dealer-advances.prompt.value: The dealer wins a hand. Who deals the next hand?

learn.mcr.match.q-match-hands.explanatio.value: A full match has four rounds — East, South, West and North — with four hands in each round, which makes sixteen hands.

learn.mcr.match.q-match-hands.hint.value: Multiply the number of rounds in a full match by the number of dealer turns in each round.

learn.mcr.match.q-match-hands.prompt.value: How many hands are played in a full match?

learn.mcr.match.step01.text.value: A match is the whole contest: a series of hands played until every player has dealt in every round. A full match has four rounds — East, South, West and North, the four winds shown here in order — and each round has four hands, one with each player as dealer. Four rounds of four hands make sixteen hands in a full match. Shorter matches that stop after the East round, or after East and South, use exactly the same rules for every hand.

learn.mcr.match.step02.text.value: The deal moves after every single hand. When a hand ends — whether the dealer won it, another player won it, or the wall ran out with no winner — the next player in turn order becomes the dealer for the next hand. The dealer never keeps the deal for a repeat hand, so a round of four hands always gives each player exactly one turn as dealer.

learn.mcr.match.step03.text.value: Every player starts a match with a score of zero. Payments move points from the players who lost a hand to the player who won it; points are never created or destroyed, so the four scores always add up to zero. A score can fall below zero during a match, and play simply continues. At the end, the four scores are ranked from highest to lowest to give the final standings.

learn.mcr.match.step04.text.value: Look back over the whole game you have learned. Four players sit at a wall of tiles. Each holds thirteen tiles, draws and throws one away in turn, and may claim thrown tiles to meld sequences, triplets and quads — or keep a hand concealed, hidden in their own hand, instead. Thrown tiles collect in ponds, where everyone can read them, and flowers are shown and replaced as they appear.

learn.mcr.match.step05.text.value: A hand is won by completing four sets and a pair — or one of the special structures, a hand built to a special shape such as seven pairs — and its patterns are then counted in a single arrangement, with exclusions applied, bigger patterns replacing the smaller ones they already include: the fan of its patterns must reach at least eight before the points for its flowers are added. The discarder, or all three opponents on a self-draw, then pay 8 base points each plus the hand value where the split requires it, and the deal passes to the next player.

learn.mcr.match.step06.text.value: That is the complete game: read the tiles, build sets toward patterns worth eight fan or more, watch the ponds and the waits, and count every winning hand from its tiles before working out who pays what. The pattern reference from the families lesson stays available whenever you want to look a pattern up.

learn.mcr.match.title.value: The full game and looking back

learn.mcr.payments.q-transfer-count.expl.value: The sequences 7-8-9 of characters, 1-2-3 of circles and 4-5-6 of bamboo use the three number groups in three suits: Mixed Straight, 8 fan. The triplet of green dragons adds 2 fan, and the hidden win on a thrown tile adds Concealed Hand, 2 fan: 8 + 2 + 2 = 12 fan.

learn.mcr.payments.q-transfer-count.hint.value: Name each pattern the hand contains and add their values one at a time. The flower is not a pattern, so leave it out of this count.

learn.mcr.payments.q-transfer-count.prom.value: How many fan do the pictured hand's patterns add up to?

learn.mcr.payments.q-transfer-discarder-.value: The hand value is 12 fan plus one flower point: 13 points. On a win from a thrown tile, the player who threw it pays the 8 base points plus the full hand value: 8 + 13 = 21 points.
Build the payment in the order this lesson teaches: work out the hand value first, from its patterns and its flower, then apply the payment split for a win on a thrown tile.
That hand's patterns add to 12 fan and its player showed one flower. It was won on a thrown tile. How many points does the player who threw the winning tile pay?

learn.mcr.payments.q-transfer-selfdraw-t.value: The hand is Seven Pairs, worth 24 fan. It contains no honors at all, which adds No Honors for 1 fan, and winning on your own draw adds Self-Drawn for 1 fan: 26 fan in total, with no flowers. On a self-draw each of the three opponents pays 8 + 26 = 34 points, so the winner receives 3 × 34 = 102 points.
Count the hand's patterns first, including what winning on your own draw adds to this structure. Then use the self-draw payment split, in which every opponent pays the same amount.
How many points does the winner of the pictured hand receive in total?

learn.mcr.payments.q-worked-discarder-pa.value: The discarder pays the 8 base points plus the full hand value of 14, which is 22. The 38 is what the winner receives from all three players together.
Build the discarder's payment from the two parts every payment has: the base points every loser pays, plus the hand value — and remember who pays the hand value on a discard win.
For the worked hand in this lesson — 12 fan, two flowers, won on a thrown tile — how many points does the discarder pay?

learn.mcr.payments.q-worked-selfdraw-tot.value: On a self-draw each of the three opponents pays 8 base + 14 hand value = 22 points, so the winner receives 3 × 22 = 66 points.
On a self-draw there is no single discarder: work out what one opponent pays, then multiply by the number of opponents.
The same hand value of 14 points is won by self-draw. How many points does the winner receive in total?

learn.mcr.payments.step01.text.value: This lesson scores one complete hand from its tiles to its payments — the hand you have followed through the course. Read it once more: the sequences 1-2-3 of characters, 4-5-6 of circles and 7-8-9 of bamboo; a triplet of red dragons; and a pair of white dragons. It was kept hidden, and it was won on a tile another player threw away. The player also showed two flowers during the hand.

learn.mcr.payments.step02.text.value: Count its patterns first. The three sequences use the number groups 1-2-3, 4-5-6 and 7-8-9 in three different suits: that is Mixed Straight, worth 8 fan. Running total: 8 fan.

learn.mcr.payments.step03.text.value: The triplet of red dragons is the pattern Dragon Pung, worth 2 fan — running total 10. The hand was kept hidden and won on a thrown tile: Concealed Hand, worth 2 fan — running total 12. No other pattern in the hand survives the exclusion rules, so its patterns add to exactly 12 fan.

learn.mcr.payments.step04.text.value: Check the gate before any money moves: 12 fan is at least the minimum of eight, so the hand is eligible and the win stands. Fan decides whether a hand can win.

learn.mcr.payments.step05.text.value: Only now are the two shown flowers added, one point each, giving a hand value of 12 + 2 = 14 points. Fan plus flowers decides what the hand is worth.

learn.mcr.payments.step06.text.value: Payments follow one base rule and one split. The base rule: every player who did not win pays 8 base points toward the win. The split is about the hand value. If the win came from another player's thrown tile, that one player — the discarder — also pays the full hand value, and the other two players pay only their 8 base points. If the winner drew the winning tile themself, there is no discarder, so every opponent pays the hand value on top of the base.

learn.mcr.payments.step07.text.value: Apply it to the worked hand, won on a thrown tile with a value of 14 points. The discarder pays 8 base + 14 hand value = 22 points. Each of the other two players pays 8 points. The winner receives 22 + 8 + 8 = 38 points in total.

learn.mcr.payments.step08.text.value: The same hand value won by self-draw instead: each of the three opponents pays 8 base + 14 hand value = 22 points, and the winner receives 22 + 22 + 22 = 66 points. Self-draw wins pay more because the hand value is collected three times instead of once. Being the dealer makes no difference to any of these amounts — the deal carries no multiplier.

learn.mcr.payments.step09.text.value: A smaller example, with the same shape of arithmetic: a hand worth eight fan with two flowers has a value of 10 points. Won on a thrown tile, the discarder pays 8 + 10 = 18 points and the other two players pay 8 each, so the winner receives 18 + 8 + 8 = 34 points. Every payment in this game can be checked the same way: base 8 for every loser, plus the hand value from the discarder alone or from everyone on a self-draw.

learn.mcr.payments.step12.text.value: Now a hand this course has never counted. Read the pictured hand yourself — name each set and the pair from the faces. It was kept hidden and won on a tile another player threw away, and its player showed one flower during the hand. Count it before answering.

learn.mcr.payments.step15.text.value: One more new count. Read the pictured hand from its faces and name its structure before answering. Its player drew the winning tile themself, and showed no flowers.

learn.mcr.sequences.q-all-chows-pair.cho.value: Yes — four sequences are all the pattern asks for
No — All Chows also requires the pair to be a suited tile, and this pair is honors
Yes — a pair of honors counts as suited for this pattern
No — All Chows requires all four sequences to be in one suit

learn.mcr.sequences.q-all-chows-pair.exp.value: All Chows needs four sequences and a pair of suited tiles. An honor pair breaks it, even with four perfect sequences.

learn.mcr.sequences.q-all-chows-pair.hin.value: All Chows restricts two things: what the four sets are, and what the pair is made of. Check the pair in the picture.

learn.mcr.sequences.q-all-chows-pair.pro.value: Does the pictured hand have the pattern All Chows?

learn.mcr.sequences.q-double-chow-value..value: The same numbers appear in two different suits, which makes the double mixed rather than pure: Mixed Double Chow, worth 1 fan.
The two sequences have the same numbers. Decide whether they share one suit or use two different suits, then use the value taught for that arrangement.
The row shows 3-4-5 of characters beside 3-4-5 of circles. Which pattern is that, and what is it worth?

learn.mcr.sequences.q-mixed-straight-id..value: The three number groups 1-2-3, 4-5-6 and 7-8-9 are spread across three different suits, which makes the straight mixed rather than pure. The hand totals 12 fan.
The word to decide is pure or mixed: count how many different suits the three number groups use.
The sequences 1-2-3 of circles, 4-5-6 of bamboo and 7-8-9 of characters, taken together, form which pattern?

learn.mcr.sequences.q-mixed-triple-value.value: The same sequence, 3-4-5, appears once in each of the three suits: Mixed Triple Chow, worth 8 fan. In one suit only it would have been the pure version, worth more.
Count how many suits the three identical sequences use, and whether their numbers are the same or shifting from one sequence to the next.
The pictured hand holds the sequence 3-4-5 in characters, in circles and in bamboo. Which pattern do those three sequences form, and what is it worth?

learn.mcr.sequences.q-pure-shifted-count.value: The character sequences are 2-3-4, 3-4-5 and 4-5-6: their starts climb by one, all in one suit. That is Pure Shifted Chows, worth 16 fan.

Group the character tiles into their three sequences and look at how their starting numbers relate to each other, and how many suits they use. Then compare that arrangement with the patterns named in this lesson.
How many fan is the pattern formed by the three character sequences in the pictured hand worth?

learn.mcr.sequences.step01.text.value: The sequences family rewards how sequences relate to each other. Read this pictured hand: 1-2-3, 4-5-6 and 7-8-9 all in characters, then 2-3-4 of circles and a pair of 5s of bamboo. The three character sequences cover the whole suit from 1 to 9 in one suit: that is the pattern Pure Straight, worth 16 fan. With its hidden discard win and its all-sequence shape also counted, the hand totals 20 fan. The smaller patterns hiding inside a straight — two sequences covering six numbers, or the 1-2-3 and 7-8-9 at its ends — are not added on top of it.

learn.mcr.sequences.step02.text.value: Read this pictured hand: 7-8-9 of characters, 1-2-3 and 2-3-4 of circles, 4-5-6 of bamboo, and a pair of 6s of bamboo. Take one sequence from each suit — 1-2-3 of circles, 4-5-6 of bamboo and 7-8-9 of characters: the same three number groups as a Pure Straight, but spread over three suits instead of one. That is the pattern Mixed Straight, worth 8 fan, and with its hidden discard win and all-sequence shape the hand totals 12 fan.

learn.mcr.sequences.step03.text.value: Some sequence patterns are about sequences that shift. Read this row as three separate groups: 2-3-4 of characters, then 3-4-5 of characters, then 4-5-6 of characters. Each group starts one number higher than the one before, and all three are in one suit. Three sequences in one suit whose starts climb by one like this form the pattern Pure Shifted Chows, worth 16 fan.

learn.mcr.sequences.step04.text.value: The shift can also be two numbers at a time. Read this row as three groups in one suit: 2-3-4, then 4-5-6, then 6-7-8 of characters — each starts two numbers higher than the one before. That is the same pattern, Pure Shifted Chows, still worth 16 fan.

learn.mcr.sequences.step05.text.value: Spread the shifting arrangement over three suits and the pattern changes. Read this row as three groups: 2-3-4 of characters, 3-4-5 of circles and 4-5-6 of bamboo. The starts still climb by one, but each sequence is in a different suit. That is the pattern Mixed Shifted Chows, worth 6 fan.

learn.mcr.sequences.step06.text.value: A sequence can also repeat exactly. Read this row as three groups with the same numbers, 3-4-5, once in each suit: characters, circles and bamboo. The same sequence in all three suits is the pattern Mixed Triple Chow, worth 8 fan.

learn.mcr.sequences.step07.text.value: The same sequence three times in one suit is worth more. Read this row as three groups of 3-4-5, all in characters. That is the pattern Pure Triple Chow, worth 24 fan.

learn.mcr.sequences.step08.text.value: Two copies of the same sequence are a smaller combination. This row shows 3-4-5 of characters twice, as two separate groups. Two identical sequences in the same suit form the pattern Pure Double Chow, worth 1 fan.

learn.mcr.sequences.step09.text.value: This row shows two groups with the same numbers in different suits: 3-4-5 of characters beside 3-4-5 of circles. That is the pattern Mixed Double Chow, worth 1 fan.

learn.mcr.sequences.step10.text.value: Two more small combinations pair up sequences in one suit. This row shows two groups: 1-2-3 and 7-8-9 of characters — the two end sequences of one suit, held together. That is the pattern Two Terminal Chows, worth 1 fan.

learn.mcr.sequences.step11.text.value: This row shows two groups in one suit: 2-3-4 and 5-6-7 of characters. Together they cover six numbers in a row. That is the pattern Short Straight, worth 1 fan.

learn.mcr.sequences.step12.text.value: You have already counted this hand once, in the lesson on the fan minimum: four sequences and a suited pair, worth 6 fan in total. Its all-sequence shape is the pattern All Chows, worth 2 of those fan — and All Chows requires the pair to be a suited tile. The same four sequences with a pair of honors would not have All Chows at all.

learn.mcr.sequences.step13.text.value: The hand below was counted in this lesson. Look at its three suits before choosing.

learn.mcr.sequences.step14.text.value: Four sequences are shown below, with a pair of East winds.

learn.mcr.sequences.step15.text.value: A new hand, never counted in this course. Read its faces yourself and group its character tiles into sequences before answering.

learn.mcr.sequences.step16.text.value: Another new hand. Find the three sequences with the same numbers before answering.

learn.mcr.specials.q-lesser-knitted-coun.value: The hand holds fourteen different tiles: eight knitted suited tiles and six different honors. With fewer than all seven honors it is Lesser Honors and Knitted Tiles, worth 12 fan, and its suited tiles do not complete the full nine-tile body, so no second structure pattern is added.
Count the honors in the picture, and compare the hand with the two knitted structures taught in this lesson: how many honors does each one need, and is the suited body complete here?
How many fan does the pictured hand score in total?

learn.mcr.specials.q-orphans-kinds.expla.value: Six terminal kinds — the 1 and 9 of each suit — plus four winds and three dragons make thirteen kinds. One of the thirteen is then held twice.

learn.mcr.specials.q-orphans-kinds.hint.value: Count the kinds in groups: the terminals of the three suits first, then the winds, then the dragons.

learn.mcr.specials.q-orphans-kinds.promp.value: How many different kinds of tile does Thirteen Orphans use, before one of them is duplicated?

learn.mcr.specials.q-seven-pairs-count.e.value: Seven Pairs is worth 24 fan. The hand contains no honors at all, which adds the pattern No Honors, worth 1 fan: 24 + 1 = 25 fan.

learn.mcr.specials.q-seven-pairs-count.h.value: First name the structure the seven pairs form and its value. Then check the hand once more for a small extra pattern: look at which kinds of tiles are present, and which are absent entirely.

learn.mcr.specials.q-seven-pairs-count.p.value: How many fan does the pictured hand score in total?

learn.mcr.specials.q-seven-pairs-value.e.value: Seven Pairs is worth 24 fan. The 88-fan figure in this lesson belongs to Seven Shifted Pairs and to Thirteen Orphans.

learn.mcr.specials.q-seven-pairs-value.h.value: Two values were named in this lesson for pair structures: the plain seven pairs, and the shifted version in one suit, which is worth much more.

learn.mcr.specials.q-seven-pairs-value.p.value: How many fan is the Seven Pairs structure worth?

learn.mcr.specials.step01.text.value: Some hands do not use sets at all. Read this pictured hand: pairs of the 1 and 2 of characters, the 3 and 4 of circles, the 5 and 6 of bamboo, and a pair of red dragons — seven pairs and nothing else. That is the special structure Seven Pairs, worth 24 fan. A hand going for seven pairs must stay hidden, because claiming a thrown tile would meld a set and break the structure. In these rules, four copies of one tile may be counted as two pairs.

learn.mcr.specials.step02.text.value: Read this pictured hand: seven pairs of characters, running 1, 1, 2, 2, 3, 3 all the way to 7, 7 — seven pairs of consecutive numbers in one suit. That is Seven Shifted Pairs, worth 88 fan. It replaces Seven Pairs rather than adding to it: the smaller structure it contains is not paid for twice, which is the exclusion rule from the earlier lesson at work.

learn.mcr.specials.step03.text.value: Read this pictured hand: the 1 and 9 of characters, the 1 and 9 of circles, the 1 and 9 of bamboo, all four winds, all three dragons — and one of those thirteen kinds twice, here a second red dragon. That is Thirteen Orphans, worth 88 fan: one of every terminal and honor kind, plus a duplicate of any one of them. It is a hidden hand with no sets, no sequences and no triplets.

learn.mcr.specials.step04.text.value: The last special structures are knitted hands, built from tiles that deliberately do not form sets. A knitted body takes the numbers 1, 4 and 7 in one suit, 2, 5 and 8 in a second suit, and 3, 6 and 9 in the third suit — this row shows 1-4-7 of characters, 2-5-8 of circles and 3-6-9 of bamboo. Side by side the numbers climb 1 to 9, but no three of them in one suit are consecutive, so nothing here is a sequence.

learn.mcr.specials.step05.text.value: Add honors to a knitted body and you get the knitted structures. Read this pictured hand: the nine knitted suited tiles and five different honors — fourteen different tiles, with no pair and no set. This structure is the pattern Lesser Honors and Knitted Tiles, worth 12 fan. Because its suited tiles are the complete knitted body — every number from 1 to 9 exactly once across the three suits — the hand also earns the pattern Knitted Straight, worth 12 fan, so its two structure patterns give 24 fan together. Any repeated tile breaks these structures, and claiming a thrown tile to meld a set ends the attempt.

learn.mcr.specials.step06.text.value: When all seven honors are present, the structure is worth more. Read this pictured hand: seven knitted suited tiles — 1, 4 and 7 of characters, 2, 5 and 8 of circles, and the 3 of bamboo — together with all seven honors: East, South, West, North and the three dragons. Fourteen different tiles again, but now every honor is there. That is the pattern Greater Honors and Knitted Tiles, worth 24 fan. It replaces the lesser knitted pattern rather than adding to it.

learn.mcr.specials.step07.text.value: The complete knitted body can also stand beside ordinary groups. Read this pictured hand: the nine knitted tiles, then an ordinary sequence, 3-4-5 of circles, and a pair of 2s of circles. The nine knitted tiles are the pattern Knitted Straight, worth 12 fan — the same pattern the lesser knitted hand above earned from its complete body. Here it is part of a hand that also holds a set and a pair, instead of a hand made only of single tiles.

learn.mcr.specials.step08.text.value: The pictured hand is the orphans hand from this lesson.

learn.mcr.specials.step10.text.value: A new knitted hand, never counted in this course. Count its honors and check whether its suited tiles complete the full nine-tile body before answering.

learn.practice.a-terminal-is-the-1-or-th.value: A terminal is the 1 or the 9 of a numbered suit. Winds and dragons are honors, not terminals.

learn.practice.a-tile-in-that-opponents-.value: A tile in that opponent's own discard pond cannot complete their hand — that is furiten. A tile with no such guarantee is not safe.

learn.practice.an-improving-tile-must-co.value: An improving tile must complete the hand and still have a copy you have not seen. Count the copies in your hand and among the visible tiles.

learn.practice.check-every-tile-in-the-h.value: Check every tile in the hand: a yaku based on simples allows no terminals and no honors anywhere.

learn.practice.chiitoitsu-is-2-han-and-e.value: Chiitoitsu is 2 han and exactly 25 fu. Base 25 × 16 = 400; a nondealer ron is 400 × 4 = 1,600.

learn.practice.count-shanten-for-the-spe.value: Count shanten for the special shapes too, not only for four sets and a pair.

learn.practice.count-the-sets-three-iden.value: Count the sets: three identical tiles, or three in a row in one suit, make a set. A complete hand is four sets plus one pair.

learn.practice.does-this-hand-have-a-com.value: Does this hand have a complete shape?
Does this hand have a complete shape? This question does not establish a legal win.

learn.practice.east-white-dragon-and-red.value: East, white dragon, and red dragon are honors; numbered tiles are suited tiles.

learn.practice.every-tile-is-a-simple-so.value: Every tile is a simple, so tanyao applies. The dot triplet rules out pinfu; riichi was not declared.

learn.practice.four-sets-are-complete-an.value: Four sets are complete. Another 5m makes the pair, so this hand is tenpai: zero shanten.

learn.practice.honors-are-the-four-winds.value: Honors are the four winds and the three dragons. A tile with a suit and a number is a suited tile, not an honor.

learn.practice.how-many-shanten-is-this-.value: How many shanten is this 13-tile hand?
How many shanten is this hand, considering special shapes?

How many total points does a nondealer collect for this seven-pairs ron, with no bonuses?

learn.practice.identify-every-yaku-for-t.value: Identify every yaku for this closed ron hand, won on 4m without riichi.

learn.practice.look-at-the-one-unfinishe.value: Look at the one unfinished part of the hand. A two-sided sequence wait can be completed from either end.

learn.practice.look-for-a-special-shape-.value: Look for a special shape as well as sets: seven different pairs also form a complete hand.

learn.practice.only-5m-completes-the-pai.value: Only 5m completes the pair. One is in hand and two are visible, leaving one unseen copy; its actual location is unknown.
Only 5m completes the pair. The three sequences and red-dragon triplet are already complete.

learn.practice.only-ranks-1-and-9-of-the.value: Only ranks 1 and 9 of the three suits are terminals. Winds are honors.

learn.practice.riichi-and-pinfu-give-2-h.value: Riichi and pinfu give 2 han. Closed ron gives 30 fu: 30 × 2^(2+2) = 480 base; 480 × 4 rounds to 2,000.

learn.practice.select-candidate-types-gu.value: Select candidate types guaranteed safe against this riichi opponent's ron. No safety is claimed against the others.

learn.practice.select-every-tile-type-th.value: Select every tile type that completes the shape, regardless of unseen copies.

learn.practice.select-improving-tile-typ.value: Select improving tile types with at least one unseen copy. Two 5m are visible outside your hand.

learn.practice.seven-different-pairs-for.value: Seven different pairs form chiitoitsu, a special closed-hand shape.

learn.practice.seven-pairs-has-its-own-f.value: Seven pairs has its own fixed fu. Use that fu with its han in the base-points formula, then multiply for a ron.

learn.practice.shanten-counts-how-many-t.value: Shanten counts how many tile changes separate the hand from a complete shape. A hand one tile away from finishing is tenpai.

learn.practice.six-pairs-and-a-single-we.value: Six pairs and a single West are tenpai for seven different pairs. Another West completes it.

learn.practice.the-incomplete-45m-sequen.value: The incomplete 45m sequence accepts 3m or 6m. The other three sets and pair are complete.

learn.practice.try-adding-each-tile-kind.value: Try adding each tile kind in turn: a wait is a kind that turns this hand into four sets and a pair.

learn.riichi.tu1.objective0.value: Tell the three suits apart and read each tile's number

learn.riichi.tu1.step01.text.value: Mahjong is played with tiles. A tile's face tells you what it is: this face shows five circles, so this tile is the 5 of dots.

learn.riichi.tu1.step02.text.value: Tiles come in three suits — three groups of tiles that share one kind of face. The first suit is dots, numbered 1 to 9. Read a dots tile by counting its circles: the number of circles is the tile's number.

learn.riichi.tu1.step03.text.value: Tap every dots tile — the tiles whose faces are made of circles.

learn.riichi.tu1.step03.wrongNote.value: Not that one — a dots tile's face is circles. Count the circles to read its number.

learn.riichi.tu1.step04.text.value: The second suit is bamboo, numbered 1 to 9. Read a bamboo tile by counting its green sticks: the number of sticks is the tile's number. One exception: the 1 of bamboo, first in this row, is a picture of a bird — it has no sticks to count.

learn.riichi.tu1.step05.text.value: Tap every bamboo tile — the tiles with the green sticks.

learn.riichi.tu1.step05.wrongNote.value: Not that one — bamboo tiles are the green sticks.

learn.riichi.tu1.step06.text.value: The third suit is characters, numbered 1 to 9. A characters tile has a two-part face: the dark character on top is the number, and the red character below is the suit's mark — it means ten thousand, and it is the same on every characters tile. The top characters are numbers written in Chinese: one line is 1, two lines are 2, three lines are 3. This row runs 1 to 9, left to right.

learn.riichi.tu1.step07.text.value: Here are all nine characters tiles again, labelled in order: 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7, 8, 9, left to right. To read a characters tile, look only at the small dark character on top — that character is the number. The red mark below is the same on all nine, so it never tells you the number. For 1, 2, and 3 you can count the lines; for the rest, match the top character against this labelled row until the faces are familiar.

learn.riichi.tu1.step08.text.value: Two characters faces are easy to mix up: the 6 and the 9. Here they are side by side — the 6 on the left, the 9 on the right. Compare only the top characters: the 6's top character ends in two separate short legs at the bottom, while the 9's top character is one long stroke that bends down and ends in a hook, with nothing separate below it. No drill in this lesson uses a 6 or a 9 until you have seen them side by side like this.

learn.riichi.tu1.step09.text.value: Tap every characters tile — the two-part faces with the red mark at the bottom.

learn.riichi.tu1.step09.wrongNote.value: Not that one — a characters tile has two parts: a dark number character on top and the red mark below it.

learn.riichi.tu1.step10.text.value: Seven tiles belong to no suit. They are honors, and they have no numbers. Four of them are winds, named for the compass points: East, South, West, and North. Each wind's face is a single dark character. This row shows them in that order: East, South, West, North.

learn.riichi.tu1.step11.text.value: Tap the East wind — the first of the four wind faces in the row you were just shown, in the order East, South, West, North.

learn.riichi.tu1.step11.wrongNote.value: Not that one — the winds in order are East, South, West, North, and East is the first face in that row.

learn.riichi.tu1.step12.text.value: Tap the North wind — the last of the four wind faces in that row.

learn.riichi.tu1.step12.wrongNote.value: Not that one — the winds in order are East, South, West, North, and North is the last face in that row.

learn.riichi.tu1.step13.text.value: The other three honors are dragons. The red dragon's face is a red character. The green dragon's face is a green character. The white dragon's face is blank, inside a frame.

learn.riichi.tu1.step14.text.value: Tap every honor tile — the winds and the dragons.

learn.riichi.tu1.step14.wrongNote.value: Not that one — honors are the winds and the dragons. They have no numbers.

learn.riichi.tu1.step15.text.value: The 1 and the 9 of each suit have a name: terminals. They are the tiles at the two ends of a suit. This row shows all six: the 1 and the 9 of characters, of dots, and of bamboo.

learn.riichi.tu1.step16.text.value: Every numbered tile from 2 to 8 is a simple. Simples are the middle tiles of a suit — every suited tile that is not a terminal.

learn.riichi.tu1.step17.text.value: Tap every terminal tile — the 1s and the 9s.

learn.riichi.tu1.step17.wrongNote.value: Not that one — a terminal is only the 1 or the 9 of a suit.

learn.riichi.tu1.step18.text.value: There are four copies of every tile: 34 kinds of tile, four copies each, 136 tiles in all. The four copies of a kind are identical, so any copy can stand in for another.

learn.riichi.tu1.step19.text.value: One 5 in each suit is printed on a red-tinted tile instead of a plain one. It is still a 5 of its suit in every way, but it is worth a bonus when it ends up in a winning hand. That bonus is explained in 'Ways to win'.

learn.riichi.tu1.step20.text.value: Tiles also have short written codes. You will see them wherever the app names a tile in text — in tile labels for screen readers, and in Practice. A suited tile's code is its number plus a suit letter: m for characters, p for dots, s for bamboo. So 3m is the 3 of characters, 3p is the 3 of dots, and 3s is the 3 of bamboo. The winds are E, S, W, and N, for East, South, West, and North. The dragons are Wh for the white dragon, Gr for the green dragon, and Rd for the red dragon. A red five's code adds the letter r: 5pr is the red 5 of dots.

learn.riichi.tu10.step01.text.value: American mahjong is a different game played with a similar set of tiles. This lesson lists the differences only. Everything in the other lessons is riichi.

learn.riichi.tu10.step02.text.value: No jokers. American sets include joker tiles, which can stand for other tiles. Riichi has no jokers: every tile is itself, and the full set is the 136 tiles from the first lesson.

learn.riichi.tu10.step03.text.value: No Charleston. American play begins with the Charleston, a passing of tiles between players. Riichi has no passing: you are dealt 13 tiles, and the hand begins.

learn.riichi.tu10.step04.text.value: No annual card. In American mahjong, the winning hands are printed on a card that is published each year. Riichi has no card: any hand with the complete shape and a yaku wins, and the yaku are the patterns from 'Ways to win'.

learn.riichi.tu10.step05.correctNote.value: Correct — that is the right answer. There is no card at all: riichi's scoring patterns are the yaku, built from any tiles, and they do not change from year to year.

learn.riichi.tu10.step05.option1.label.value: Scoring patterns — yaku — built from any tiles

learn.riichi.tu10.step05.text.value: What takes the place of the annual card here?

learn.riichi.tu10.step05.wrongNote.value: There is no card at all here, and nothing about what a winning hand must contain changes from year to year or from hand to hand. Think back to the 'Ways to win' lesson: what must every winning hand contain?

learn.riichi.tu10.step06.text.value: When the American variant arrives it will have its own lessons. Everything before this lesson was riichi.

learn.riichi.tu2.covered0.value: A standard winning shape is four sets and a pair

learn.riichi.tu2.covered1.value: A set is a sequence or a triplet

learn.riichi.tu2.covered2.value: Seven pairs and thirteen orphans are the special shapes

learn.riichi.tu2.objective1.value: Distinguish a complete standard shape from an incomplete shape

learn.riichi.tu2.step01.text.value: You hold 13 tiles. A hand wins when it becomes 14 tiles arranged in one particular shape. This lesson names the parts of that shape, one at a time.

learn.riichi.tu2.step02.text.value: The shape is built from groups of three tiles: sets. One kind of set is a sequence — three tiles in a row in one suit. This is a sequence: 3, 4, 5 of dots.

learn.riichi.tu2.step03.text.value: The other kind of set is a triplet — three copies of the same tile. This is a triplet: three 9s of bamboo.

learn.riichi.tu2.step04.text.value: The last part of the shape is a pair — two copies of the same tile. This is a pair: two 5s of dots. A winning hand has exactly one pair.

learn.riichi.tu2.step05.text.value: Put the parts together: a complete hand is four sets and a pair, 14 tiles in all. This hand is complete — four sets, and the two 5s of dots are its pair. A tile on its own, in no set and with no matching copy beside it, is a single.

learn.riichi.tu2.step06.text.value: Which of these is a set?

learn.riichi.tu2.step06.wrongNote.value: Those skip a number — a sequence is three in a row, with no gaps.

learn.riichi.tu2.step06.wrongNote-2.value: That is a pair — two copies of the same tile. A pair is part of the shape, but it is not a set.

learn.riichi.tu2.step06.wrongNote-3.value: That is only two tiles — a set has three tiles.

learn.riichi.tu2.step07.wrongNote.value: Count the tiles in that row — a complete hand has one more tile than that.

learn.riichi.tu2.step07.wrongNote-2.value: Count the groups in that row, then count its tiles: a complete hand needs one part that this row leaves no room for.

learn.riichi.tu2.step07.wrongNote-3.value: Count the groups and count the tiles in that row — compare both counts with the shape taught at the start of this lesson.

learn.riichi.tu2.step08.text.value: Two more shapes also win. Seven pairs: seven different pairs and nothing else. Thirteen orphans: one of every terminal and every honor, with one of them twice, as the pair. Most winning hands use the standard shape — four sets and a pair — so that shape comes first.

learn.riichi.tu3.completion.value: Make six legal discards and finish the turn explanation.

learn.riichi.tu3.covered0.value: Draw one tile, discard one tile

learn.riichi.tu3.covered2.value: Table furniture: seat winds, the round label, the wall and its count, the dora indicator, the honba counter, 25,000 starting points

learn.riichi.tu3.objective0.value: Discard legal tiles on the real table

learn.riichi.tu3.step01.text.value: Your hand is at the bottom of the table, and the other three players sit around it. A turn works like this: you draw one tile — take it from the face-down tiles — and then you discard one tile: tap a tile in your hand to throw it away. Drawing and then discarding keeps your hand at 13 tiles while you build toward four sets and a pair. The table itself is in front of you as you read, and this step names everything on it. One player in each hand is the dealer: the player sitting in the East seat for that hand. The dealer deals the tiles and takes the first turn, and turns then pass round the table in the order East, South, West, North. Each player has a name chip showing a wind — East, South, West, or North: that wind is the player's seat wind, the wind of the seat they are sitting in, counted round from the dealer — the dealer is East, the next player round is South, then West, then North. Your chip reads 'East · You', so your seat wind is East for this hand, and you are the dealer. The label in the middle of the table, 'East 1', names the round and the hand. Its first word is the round wind: the wind that names the whole round, the same for all four players at once. So 'East 1' means the East round, hand 1 — and if the middle label reads East while your own chip reads South, that means the round wind is East and your seat wind is South: you are not the dealer, the East player is. The two winds do different jobs: the round wind names the round, and your seat wind says where you sit in it and when you play. Keeping three copies of the round wind, or of your own seat wind, is also worth extra value when a hand is scored — 'Ways to win' teaches that pattern. The face-down tiles are the wall, the tiles everyone draws from, and the number beside 'Wall' is how many tiles are left in it. In the middle sits one face-up tile under the label DORA: that tile is the dora indicator. It points to a bonus tile, named a dora: for a numbered tile, the dora is the next number up in the same suit, so an indicator showing the 3 of dots makes the 4 of dots a dora, and each dora in a winning hand adds to that hand's value. Beside it, the honba counter ('0 honba') counts honba, a repeat counter: it rises by one each time the dealer deals the same hand again, and each honba adds 300 points to the next winning hand. The open area in front of each player is their pond, where their discards will lie face up. Every player starts a game with 25,000 points, shown on their chip.

learn.riichi.tu3.step02.text.value: Tap a tile in your hand to discard it.

learn.riichi.tu3.step03.text.value: Draw, discard, repeat — that is the whole turn, and it is what just happened: you drew and discarded six times. Each time, your pond grew by one tile and the wall count in the middle fell as the four players drew. Your discarded tiles stay face up in front of you, in the order you discarded them: that area is your pond. All four ponds are face up for everyone to see, and later lessons will read them.

learn.riichi.tu4.completion.value: Make the requested chi, pon, and kan, then finish the explanations.

learn.riichi.tu4.covered0.value: A call claims a discard to complete a set

learn.riichi.tu4.covered1.value: Chi takes a discard from your left, for a sequence

learn.riichi.tu4.covered2.value: Pon takes any opponent's discard, for a triplet

learn.riichi.tu4.covered3.value: Kan is four of a kind; a concealed kan keeps a closed hand closed

learn.riichi.tu4.covered4.value: A kan turns over a new dora indicator; dora are bonus tiles

learn.riichi.tu4.objective0.value: Make legal chi, pon, and kan calls

learn.riichi.tu4.objective1.value: Distinguish an open call from a concealed kan

learn.riichi.tu4.step01.text.value: Tiles reach your hand by drawing. But sometimes another player discards a tile that completes a set in your hand. When that happens, you can claim the discard at once, instead of waiting to draw the tile yourself. Claiming a discard is a call. The completed set is placed face up beside your hand, and your hand is open from then on: everyone can see that set. An open hand is a hand with a set placed face up in this way. A closed hand is the opposite: no set has been placed face up, and every tile is still hidden in your hand.

learn.riichi.tu4.step02.text.value: The first call is chi. Chi claims a discard from the player on your left — only from that player — to complete a sequence. If you hold the 2 and 3 of dots, and the player on your left discards the 4 of dots, chi takes it, and you have the sequence 2, 3, 4 at once.

learn.riichi.tu4.step03.text.value: New example — this scene starts a new position on purpose. Watch the player on your left — a discard you can use is coming.

learn.riichi.tu4.step04.text.value: The second call is pon. Pon claims any player's discard to complete a triplet. If you hold two copies of a tile and any opponent discards the third copy, pon takes it at once, and the triplet is placed face up beside your hand.

learn.riichi.tu4.step05.text.value: New example — this scene starts a new position on purpose. Watch the discards — a tile you hold two copies of is coming.

learn.riichi.tu4.step06.text.value: The third call is kan: a set of four copies of the same tile. You can call kan on a discard when you hold the other three copies, or declare kan from four copies in your own hand — declaring it yourself keeps your hand closed. After a kan you draw an extra tile, because the set of four leaves your hand one tile short.

learn.riichi.tu4.step07.text.value: New example — this scene starts a new position on purpose. Watch the discards — a tile you hold three copies of is coming.

learn.riichi.tu4.step08.text.value: A kan also turns a new tile face up on the table: a dora indicator. It marks a bonus tile, a dora. For a suited tile, the dora is the next number up in the same suit — an indicator showing the 3 of dots makes the 4 of dots a dora. Each dora in a winning hand adds to the hand's score. The red-tinted 5s from the first lesson are always dora, indicator or not.

learn.riichi.tu4.step09.text.value: Chi, pon, and a kan called on a discard all open your hand: the set sits face up where everyone can see it. An open hand cannot use every way of winning — some of the winning patterns taught in 'Ways to win' need a closed hand. A kan declared from four copies in your own hand is the exception: it keeps your hand closed.

learn.riichi.tu5.completion.value: Declare both demonstrated wins and finish their explanations.

learn.riichi.tu5.covered0.value: Tenpai means one tile from a complete shape

learn.riichi.tu5.covered1.value: Your waits are the tiles that complete the hand

learn.riichi.tu5.covered2.value: Ron wins on a discard; tsumo on your own draw

learn.riichi.tu5.covered3.value: Furiten: a wait in your own pond bars ron

learn.riichi.tu5.objective1.value: Declare tsumo and ron in legal positions

learn.riichi.tu5.step01.text.value: When a hand is one tile away from the complete shape — four sets and a pair — the hand is ready. Ready has a name: tenpai. The tiles that would complete the hand are its waits. This hand is tenpai: it is waiting on the 5 of dots to make its pair.

learn.riichi.tu5.step02.text.value: A tenpai hand wins when one of its waits arrives, and the two ways to win have names. Ron: winning on a tile another player discarded — you claim that discard, and only the player who discarded it pays you. Tsumo: winning on a tile you drew yourself — all three opponents pay you. The next two scenes show one of each: first a tsumo, then a ron.

learn.riichi.tu5.step03.text.value: Your hand is tenpai. The other players take their turns; watch what you draw.

learn.riichi.tu5.step04.text.value: That was tsumo: a win on a tile you drew yourself. When you win by tsumo, all three opponents pay you — here, each paid 6,000 — and your 1,000-point riichi stake came back to you on top, so you gained 19,000 points in all. The table has already set up the next hand, which is why the tiles in front of you are different.

learn.riichi.tu5.step05.text.value: One rule limits ron: furiten. If one of your waits is a tile you discarded earlier yourself — a tile now sitting in your own pond — then you are in furiten, and you cannot ron at all, not even on a different wait. You can still win by tsumo. Furiten ends when your waits change.

learn.riichi.tu5.step06.text.value: New example — the hand has changed on purpose. You are tenpai. Watch the discards — one of your waits is coming.

learn.riichi.tu5.step07.text.value: That was ron: a win on another player's discard. Only the player who discarded the winning tile pays you — here South paid 2,900 — and your 1,000-point riichi stake came back to you on top, so you gained 3,900 points in all. The other two players paid nothing. The table has already set up the next hand, which is why the tiles in front of you are different.

learn.riichi.tu6.completion.value: Declare riichi with an eligible discard and observe the hand's outcome.

learn.riichi.tu6.covered0.value: Riichi needs a closed, ready hand, 1,000 points, and at least four live-wall tiles

learn.riichi.tu6.covered1.value: After riichi, discard drawn tiles unless winning or making a permitted concealed kan

learn.riichi.tu6.covered2.value: The next winner receives riichi sticks; a draw carries them forward

learn.riichi.tu6.objective1.value: Explain the stake and hand-lock restrictions

learn.riichi.tu6.step01.text.value: Riichi is a declaration you make while discarding, when your hand is tenpai and still closed — you have made no calls. Declaring riichi pays a stake of 1,000 points at once: the points leave your score and sit on the table as a stake stick, and the next player to win a hand collects every stake on the table. After that, your hand is locked: on each of your turns you discard the tile you drew, unless that tile wins the hand or can form a kan with copies already in your hand. In exchange, riichi itself counts as a way to score — a pattern in its own right, taught in 'Ways to win' — so a hand that has declared riichi can always win, by tsumo or by ron. You need at least 1,000 points to declare, and at least four tiles left to draw.

learn.riichi.tu6.step02.text.value: This hand is tenpai and closed, and it is your turn. One tile in your hand is marked: it is the discard that keeps the hand tenpai. Tap the marked tile: tapping it discards the tile and declares riichi with that discard, and the 1,000-point stake is paid at that moment — your score drops by 1,000 and the stake stick appears in the middle of the table. Any other discard would leave the hand more than one tile from complete, and riichi needs a tenpai hand.

learn.riichi.tu6.step03.text.value: After riichi, you discard each tile you draw, unless it wins the hand. The rest of this hand plays out by itself — watch how it ends.

learn.riichi.tu7.completion.value: Answer both yaku questions correctly and finish the six-yaku introduction.

learn.riichi.tu7.covered0.value: Riichi, tanyao, and each qualifying yakuhai are 1 han

learn.riichi.tu7.covered1.value: Pinfu needs a closed all-sequence hand, a nonvalue pair, and a two-sided wait

learn.riichi.tu7.covered2.value: Toitoi and chiitoitsu are 2 han; dora alone never permit a win

learn.riichi.tu7.objective1.value: Separate a yaku from bonus dora

learn.riichi.tu7.step01.text.value: A complete shape is not enough to win. The hand must also contain at least one yaku — a scoring pattern in the tiles. Each yaku is worth han, the units a hand's value is counted in; the next lesson turns han into points. Dora are not yaku: each dora adds 1 han as a bonus, but a hand with dora and no yaku still cannot win. This lesson introduces the patterns a beginner meets first.

learn.riichi.tu7.step02.text.value: Riichi — 1 han. The declaration from the Riichi lesson is itself a yaku: a closed hand that declares riichi has its pattern, and can win by tsumo or by ron. Furiten still limits ron.

learn.riichi.tu7.step03.text.value: Tanyao — 1 han. Every tile in the hand is a simple: no terminals and no honors anywhere in the hand.

learn.riichi.tu7.step04.text.value: Yakuhai — 1 han for a triplet or kan of dragons, of the round wind, or of your own seat wind — the wind of the seat you are sitting in. The round wind and your seat wind are the scoring winds: they are the winds that score in this pattern. A triplet that is both the round wind and your seat wind counts twice: 2 han.

learn.riichi.tu7.step05.text.value: Which yaku does this hand have?

learn.riichi.tu7.step05.wrongNote.value: The red dragons are honors — tanyao allows none.

learn.riichi.tu7.step05.wrongNote-2.value: Riichi is a declaration made during play, not a pattern you can see in these tiles. Look at the triplet in this hand, and at what kind of tile it is made of.

learn.riichi.tu7.step05.wrongNote-3.value: Pinfu is all sequences — this hand contains a triplet, so look again at what that triplet is made of.

learn.riichi.tu7.step06.text.value: Pinfu — 1 han, closed hands only. All four sets are sequences, the pair is not a dragon or a scoring wind, and the hand waits on a tile that completes a sequence from either end.

learn.riichi.tu7.step07.text.value: Which yaku does this hand have?

learn.riichi.tu7.step07.wrongNote.value: Pinfu is all sequences — this hand has a triplet of the 5 of dots.

learn.riichi.tu7.step07.wrongNote-2.value: Look for a triplet of dragons or of a scoring wind in this hand — then check what kinds of tiles make up the rest of the hand.

learn.riichi.tu7.step07.wrongNote-3.value: That pattern needs every set to be a triplet — this hand is mostly sequences. Check what kinds of tiles make up the whole hand instead.

learn.riichi.tu7.step08.text.value: Toitoi — 2 han. All four sets are triplets or kans, plus the pair. No sequences anywhere.

learn.riichi.tu7.step09.text.value: Chiitoitsu — 2 han, closed hands only. Seven different pairs instead of the standard shape. Four identical tiles count as one pair, not two.

learn.riichi.tu7.step10.text.value: A hand can hold more than one yaku at once, and then the han add up — the yaku stack. This hand is closed and all sequences, and every tile is a simple: it is read aloud as 2, 3, 4 of characters; 3, 4, 5 of dots; 6, 7, 8 of dots; 2, 3, 4 of bamboo; and a pair of 5s of characters. Counted out: pinfu — 1 han, for the all-sequence closed hand with a two-sided wait — and tanyao — 1 han, because every tile is a simple. Stacked, the hand is worth 2 han.

learn.riichi.tu7.step11.text.value: How many han is this hand worth in all? One triplet in it was called with pon, so the hand is open. It is read aloud as: three 2s of dots, three 4s of bamboo, three 6s of characters, three 8s of bamboo, and a pair of 3s of dots.

learn.riichi.tu7.step11.wrongNote.value: Count the patterns one at a time and add their values together. First check what kinds of tiles the hand is made of, then check the shape of its sets — an open hand can still hold both of those patterns.

learn.riichi.tu8.completion.value: Win the seeded hand and correctly identify its han, fu, and total received.

learn.riichi.tu8.covered0.value: Han and fu set the points

learn.riichi.tu8.covered2.value: East-only and East/South games are available; the dealer can repeat, adding honba

learn.riichi.tu8.objective0.value: Read han, fu, and payments from a real win

learn.riichi.tu8.step01.text.value: A winning hand is paid in points, and the points come from two numbers. Han counts the hand's value: each yaku gives han, and each dora adds 1 han. Fu are minipoints from the hand's shape — its triplets, its pair, its wait, and how it was won. Each extra han roughly doubles what the hand pays. This lesson wins a real hand, then reads the numbers off that win.

learn.riichi.tu8.step02.text.value: New example — the hand has changed on purpose. This hand is one tile from complete. Watch your draws: a winning tile is coming, and the questions after it are about what the win pays.

learn.riichi.tu8.step04.text.value: How many han was your hand?

learn.riichi.tu8.step04.wrongNote.value: Use the breakdown on the step before this one — tap Back to see it again. It lists every part of this same win's han, line by line, and gives the total.

learn.riichi.tu8.step05.text.value: How many fu — minipoints — did it have?

learn.riichi.tu8.step05.wrongNote.value: Use the breakdown two steps back — tap Back twice to see it again. It states this same win's fu and where the number comes from.

learn.riichi.tu8.step06.text.value: How many points did you gain?

learn.riichi.tu8.step06.wrongNote.value: Use the breakdown three steps back — tap Back to return to it. It adds up this same win: what each opponent paid, plus the riichi stake that came back to you.

learn.riichi.tu8.step07.text.value: One player in each hand is the dealer: the player sitting in the East seat for that hand. A dealer's win pays more — on a dealer tsumo, all three opponents pay the dealer rate — and a dealer also pays more when another player wins by tsumo. All payments round up to the next 100 points.

learn.riichi.tu8.step08.text.value: If the dealer wins a hand, or a hand is drawn with the dealer tenpai, the same dealer deals the next hand, and the honba count rises by one. Honba are a bonus counter: each honba adds 300 points to the next winning hand. An East-only game runs from East 1 to East 4; an East/South game continues through South 4. A game ends early if any player's score falls below zero.

learn.riichi.tu8.step09.text.value: New example — a second worked hand, counted in full on the next step. This hand is closed, and it had declared riichi. It is read aloud as: three 2s of characters; 3, 4, 5 of characters; 6, 7, 8 of dots; three 9s of bamboo; and a pair of white dragons. It won by ron — on a discard — when the white dragon arrived: the hand had been waiting on that one tile alone to complete its pair. You sit in the South seat, so you are not the dealer. There are no dora in the hand and no honba.

learn.riichi.tu8.step10.text.value: Here is that hand counted out in full. Han first: riichi — 1 han, for the declaration. No other pattern is in the hand, and there are no dora, so the hand is 1 han in all. Now the fu, part by part. Every hand starts with a base of 20 fu. Winning by ron with a closed hand adds 10 fu. A closed triplet of simples adds 4 fu: the three 2s of characters. A closed triplet of terminals adds 8 fu: the three 9s of bamboo. A pair of dragons adds 2 fu. Waiting on one tile alone — the pair tile — adds 2 fu. The sequences add nothing. The parts add to 46 fu, and fu always round up to the next ten, so the hand counts as 50 fu. At 1 han and 50 fu, a win by ron for a player who is not the dealer pays 1,600 points, and the player who discarded the winning tile pays all of it.

learn.riichi.tu8.step11.text.value: How many han was the worked hand?

learn.riichi.tu8.step11.wrongNote.value: Use the breakdown on the step before this one — tap Back to see it again. It lists every part of this same hand's han, line by line, and gives the total.

learn.riichi.tu8.step12.text.value: How many fu did the worked hand have, after rounding?
